title: I Now Pronounce You Chuck and Larry
full_review:
Making a mockery of comedy more than matrimony, the puerile "I Now Pronounce You Chuck & Larry" (Universal) fails to mine much humor from the premise of best friends pretending to be gay so they can qualify for domestic partnership benefits.
Perhaps it was unreasonable to expect subtlety or wit from Adam Sandler's production company, despite his above-par work in recent films like "Spanglish" and "Reign Over Me."

Here, reverting to his comic persona of yore, he's ill-equipped to treat this theme (or homosexuality in general) with anything other than crude and sometimes brutal obviousness, such as trying to score easy laughs by stereotyping a boy who prefers theater to sports.

But it's the movie's raunchiness and extolling of rough intimacy that is more offensive that what it says or implies about the sanctity of marriage, though the morally relativistic grounds cited for its message of acceptance will give faithful viewers pause.

"I Now Pronounce You Chuck & Larry" seems to want to have it both ways by being outwardly homophobic and advocating gay marriage. It also exonerates its protagonists from breaking the law and perpetrating a fraud more serious than lying about their sexual orientation.

Brooklyn firefighters Chuck Levine (Sandler) and Larry Valentine (Kevin James from TV's "The King of Queens") are partners on the job and best of friends off, despite differing lifestyles. Chuck is a playboy, while Larry is a widower scrambling to raise two young children, including Eric (Cole Morgen) the boy mentioned above.

Due to bureaucratic red tape concerning pension beneficiaries, Larry asks Chuck to enter into a legal union so his kids will be protected. A reluctant Chuck agrees only after Larry saves his life, but the ruse gets complicated. With a rabid city inspector (Steve Buscemi) investigating their case, they must prove they're a legitimate gay couple. On the advice of their attorney, Alex McDonough (Jessica Biel), they marry in Canada and Chuck moves into Larry's house.

Three screenwriters and director Dennis Dugan try to cover all the bases with their overly long and complex story, one crammed with lifeless tangents. Naturally, the duo is publicly exposed and must deal with firehouse colleagues, one of whom, Duncan (Ving Rhames), comes out of the closet. Chuck has difficulty disguising his attraction to their lawyer, and there's even the obligatory shower scene at the firehouse.

In addition to the litany of objectionable material, there's one relevant exchange about religion. Chuck says he wants a Jewish wedding ceremony so as not to offend his mother. Larry responds that he's Catholic and is afraid of offending Mel Gibson by not having a Catholic rite.

The film contains pervasive sexual content and references, frequent crude and crass language, one instance of profanity, vulgar gestures, some bathroom humor, fondling of a woman's breasts, rear male nudity, much skimpy female costuming, frequent racial, gender and homophobic slurs, a drug reference, and much violence including fisticuffs. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
